bridges.description: Establish that deterministic causation is compatible with the kind of free will worth having.
Connect responsiveness to reasons, foresight, and self-control to agency and responsibility.
Explain free will as an evolved skill strengthened by education and social institutions.
Show how graded capacities support fair, humane, and instrumental accountability practices.
Argue that choices do not constitute free will because agents did not control the causes that formed their chooser and values.
Trace behavior through an unbroken biological and environmental history rather than an independent source of action.
Treat self-control itself as a biologically developed trait whose distribution is not chosen.
Connect reduced responsibility judgments to less cruel institutions while retaining instrumental protection and incentives.

sections.title: Causal origins of agency
sections.rationale: The central clash begins with whether present intention and reasons-responsiveness suffice, or whether freedom requires control over the history that formed the intending agent.

sections.title: Evolved self-control and reasons
sections.rationale: Dennett identifies free will with an evolved capacity for foresight, reliability, reasons, and self-control; Sapolsky argues that this capacity is itself biologically caused.

sections.title: Responsibility and humane institutions
sections.rationale: Both accept instrumental sanctions but dispute whether responsibility remains justified and whether moral progress reflects improved accountability or subtraction of blame.

sections.title: Quotation, interpretation, and intuition
sections.rationale: The live exchange over the machine passage, runner analogy, two-stage model, and intuition bears directly on how each side represents and supports the rival conception.

sections.title: Determinism, choice, and unpredictability
sections.rationale: The parties agree that options and choices occur but dispute whether deterministic chaos and uncontrollable variation leave room for autonomy once the chooser's values are causally formed.

sourceSpan.excerpt: think the very last point, Dan, is there's another realm in which I think you've been seduced into a great embrace of free will, which is you've got a lot more faith in intuition than I think is justified. But you say one of its strengths is it aligns with our intuitions. Quote, that model, quote, provides some account of our important intuition that we are the authors of our moral decisions. In other words, your model for why free will is more acceptable because it fits with our intuition that we have free will. And I think my last point here that I want to make is intuition is a really lousy guide for thinking about how the world works. Let me give you an example. I will bet, Dan, if you and I were sitting in a cafe 400 years ago, we were the same people and just as reflective and we would have like given money to NPR if it existed at the time. All of that, we would have been the same reasonable people. It would have been probably intuitively obvious to us that certain people are meant to be slaves. In fact, they're so incapable of taking care of themselves, it's a blessing to enslave them and feed them and clothe them and that and that's not intuitively obvious to to us anymore. It's not intuitively obvious that it's okay to have 4-year-olds work in factories. But in the past would have seemed intuitively obvious to us as well. It's no longer intuitively obvious that a kid who has a cortical malformation and as a result reverses looped letters and has trouble learning to read because of their dyslexia, it's no longer intuitively obvious to us that they're lazy and unmotivated. But 40, 50 years ago, I suspect both of us would have found it obvious that this is a kid who just really isn't paying attention, isn't motivated. Over and over and over, our intuitions have proven wrong. Over and over, when we realize our intuitions are very poor litmus test and we recognize we are intuitively punishing and rewarding and judging and all of that for things people had no control over. Over and over, when we recognize that these intuitions, in fact, are based on responsibility, which is simply not there, the world becomes a better place. It really is a very good thing that we figured out witches don't control the weather and we figured out that rotten psychoanalytically poisonous mothers don't cause schizophrenia and that people with a certain variant of a gene for the leptin receptor have trouble having their brain satiate rather than them just hating themselves and thus eating themselves into obesity. At every one of these steps, our initial intuitions have proven very, very suspect and wrong. And at each step, when we actually learn what's going on, we we subtract responsibility out of it. And not only doesn't the societal roof fall in, it becomes a much better place to live in.
